[LLM] VS Code child process reads wallet / dev-credential files (Glassworm credential theft) Actions on Objectives Medium
Hunts for Code.exe / node.exe / electron.exe (or their child processes) reading high-value credential or wallet files within seconds of an extension directory write — the article describes trojanized extensions harvesting cryptocurrency wallets and developer credentials. Rationale: Article: 'stole cryptocurrency wallets and developer credentials'. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/ • https://chrome.google.com/webstore/detail/metamask/nkbihfbeogaeaoehlefnkodbefgpgknn

[LLM] First-time install of any Glassworm-named extension across the org (baseline anti-join) Delivery Medium
Surfaces the first organisation-wide installation of any of the eight named Glassworm extension package names. Defenders who haven't yet hit Glassworm get an early-warning signal as soon as a developer pulls a re-uploaded clone. Designed for environments where IOC names may resurface under typosquatted variants. Rationale: The eight package names are explicit Glassworm IOCs from the kill-chain block. Baseline anti-join means SOC only sees a host the *first* time it picks up a trojanized extension — avoids alert fatigue once a host is already known-compromised. Sigma omitted because anti-join over baseline is a correlation, not single-event shape. Cross-checked against: • https://open-vsx.org/ • https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1176

let Baseline = DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp between (ago(90d) .. ago(7d))
    | where FolderPath has @"\.vscode\extensions\"
    | where FolderPath has_any (GlasswormPkgs)
    | summarize by DeviceName;
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FolderPath has @"\.vscode\extensions\"
| where FolderPath has_any (GlasswormPkgs)
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on DeviceName
| summarize FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), arg_min(Timestamp, *) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| project FirstSeen, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256
| order by FirstSeen desc

let Baseline = ImFileEvent
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(90d) .. ago(7d))
    | where TargetFilePath has @"\.vscode\extensions\"
    | where TargetFilePath has_any (GlasswormPkgs)
    | summarize by DvcHostname;
ImFileEvent

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc

| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty

Seedworm APT Abuses Signed Fortemedia and SentinelOne Binaries for DLL Sideloading

Cyber Security News
2026-05-27 16 use cases 8 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A well-known Iran-linked hacking group has been caught running a far-reaching espionage campaign that touched at least nine organizations across nine countries and four continents in early 2026. [LLM] Seedworm DLL sideload via signed Fortemedia fmapp.exe loading malicious fmapp.dll Installation High
Hunts for the legitimately signed Fortemedia audio-driver utility fmapp.exe loading a sideloaded fmapp.dll that delivers ChromElevator. Pivots on the file pair, on the malicious-DLL hash, and on fmapp.exe executing from a non-standard install path. Rationale: Directly anchors on the article's named binary/DLL pair (fmapp.exe + fmapp.dll), the SHA256 of the malicious DLL (c6182fd...), and the legitimate signed loader hash (e258926...). Sideloading from a non-Program-Files path is the article's specific abuse pattern. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0069/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1574/002/
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1553.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "fmapp.exe"
| where FileName =~ "fmapp.dll"
| where SHA256 == "c6182fd01b14d84723e3c9d11bc0e16b34de6607ccb8334fc9bb97c1b44f0cde"
   or InitiatingProcessSHA256 == "e25892603c42e34bd7ba0d8ea73be600d898cadc290e3417a82c04d6281b743b"
   or InitiatingProcessFolderPath !contains "Program Files"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName endswith "fmapp.exe"
| where TargetFileName endswith "fmapp.dll"
| where TargetFileSHA256 =~ "c6182fd01b14d84723e3c9d11bc0e16b34de6607ccb8334fc9bb97c1b44f0cde"
   or not (ActingProcessName contains "Program Files")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Seedworm DLL sideload via signed SentinelOne memory scanner loading sentinelagentcore.dll Installation High
Detects the legitimately signed sentinelmemoryscanner.exe loading a sideloaded sentinelagentcore.dll outside the genuine SentinelOne installation path. The pair carries ChromElevator and is the second sideload chain Symantec attributes to this Seedworm intrusion. Rationale: Article names the exact loader binary (sentinelmemoryscanner.exe / SHA256 128b58a2...) and sideloaded DLL (sentinelagentcore.dll / SHA256 0c9b9119...). Detection forces co-occurrence of both filenames plus either hash match or execution from a non-SentinelOne path. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0069/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1574/002/
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1553.002

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "sentinelmemoryscanner.exe"
| where FileName =~ "sentinelagentcore.dll"
| where SHA256 == "0c9b911935a3705b0ad569446804d80026feb6db3884aeb240b6c76e9b8cf139"
   or InitiatingProcessSHA256 == "128b58a2a2f1df66c474094aacb7e50189025fbf45d7cd8e0834e93a8fbed667"
   or InitiatingProcessFolderPath !contains "Sentinel"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName endswith "sentinelmemoryscanner.exe"
| where TargetFileName endswith "sentinelagentcore.dll"
| where TargetFileSHA256 =~ "0c9b911935a3705b0ad569446804d80026feb6db3884aeb240b6c76e9b8cf139"

[LLM] Seedworm node.exe execution orchestrated from XML script wrapper Exploitation Medium
Hunts for node.exe being launched with an XML file argument or by an unusual parent, matching Symantec's observation that Seedworm now embeds the Node.js orchestrator script inside an XML file on disk. This replaces the actor's older raw-PowerShell loader pattern. Rationale: Anchors on the article's specific claim: 'A Node.js script was found embedded inside an XML file on one of the infected machines, silently orchestrating the entire attack.' node.exe with an .xml argument is highly unusual in enterprise environments outside known dev workflows. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0069/
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1218
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "node.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has ".xml"
   or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","explorer.exe")
| where FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files"
   or InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath,
          ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\node.exe"
| where CommandLine has ".xml"
   or ParentProcessName endswith_cs "\\wscript.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith_cs "\\cscript.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith_cs "\\mshta.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith_cs "\\cmd.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith_cs "\\powershell.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Seedworm PowerShell / curl payload retrieval from 179.43.177.220:8080 staging server Delivery High
Detects host-side downloads of nm.ps1, a.dat or a.exe from the Seedworm staging IP 179.43.177.220 on port 8080. Anchors on the exact attacker URL paths the article lists and the actor's habit of pairing PowerShell with curl to keep download activity off script-block logs. Rationale: Article lists the exact staging URL set: http://179.43.177.220:8080/nm.ps1, /a.dat, /a.exe. Pairs the IP+port with the actor's documented download tool set (PowerShell, curl) and lateral helpers (node.exe per the Node.js orchestration claim). Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0069/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1105/
ATT&CKT1105 T1059.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Endpoint.Processes
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "179.43.177.220"
| where RemotePort == 8080
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "curl.exe", "cmd.exe", "node.exe", "bitsadmin.exe", "certutil.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,

[LLM] Seedworm Run-key persistence pointing at node.exe or sideload binary path Installation High
Detects writes to HKCU/HKLM Run / RunOnce that reference node.exe, the sideloaded fmapp.exe / sentinelmemoryscanner.exe loader binaries, the malicious DLLs, or an .xml wrapper. Symantec specifically called out that Seedworm restarts the loader chain by adding a Windows startup registry entry. Rationale: Article: 'Persistence was established by adding a registry entry under the Windows startup key, ensuring the loader chain restarted each time the user logged in.' Anchors on the specific binaries / DLLs / XML wrapper named in the campaign rather than generic Run-key writes. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1547/001/

[LLM] Seedworm exfiltration to sendit.sh / svc.wompworthy.com / timetrakr.cloud Command & Control High
Detects outbound HTTP(S) to the three attacker-controlled domains named in the campaign - sendit.sh (public file-transfer used for data exfiltration), svc.wompworthy.com (C2), timetrakr.cloud (PowerShell module staging). Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT

    [| tstats `summariesonly` count

        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["e25892603c42e34bd7ba0d8ea73be600d898cadc290e3417a82c04d6281b743b", "c6182fd01b14d84723e3c9d11bc0e16b34de6607ccb8334fc9bb97c1b44f0cde", "128b58a2a2f1df66c474094aacb7e50189025fbf45d7cd8e0834e93a8fbed667", "0c9b911935a3705b0ad569446804d80026feb6db3884aeb240b6c76e9b8cf139", "74ab3838ebed7054b2254bf7d334c80c8b2cfec4a97d1706723f8ea55f11061f", "3ee7dab4ae4f6d4f16dfabb6f38faef370411a9fc00ff035844e54703b99600a", "bee79c3302b1a7afc0952842d14eff83a604ef00bfdae525176c16c80b2045f7", "d587959841a763669279ad831b8f0379f6a7b037dffc19deab5d41f37f8b5ffc", "b21c802775df0c0d82c8cfde299084abc624898b10258db641b820172a0ba29a"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] SRG/Luna Moth typosquatted IT-helpdesk lookalike domain resolution · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] SRG in-person USB exfil: mass file copy to non-system drive after remote-help tool · [LLM] SRG extortion leak-site contact: traffic to business-data-leaks.com · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
[LLM] SRG/Luna Moth typosquatted IT-helpdesk lookalike domain resolution Delivery High
Surfaces DNS resolution or HTTP traffic from any corporate endpoint to the SRG/Luna Moth typosquatted helpdesk lookalike domains named in the May 2026 FBI flash alert. Catches the lure infrastructure used to coach employees into calling fake IT support. Rationale: Domains pulled verbatim from the article IOC list (duanemorris-helpdesk.com, perkinscoie-helpdesk.com, millermartin-helpdesk.com). EclecticIQ May 2025 report and the May 2025 FBI PIN both confirm Luna Moth's pattern of registering law-firm-themed helpdesk lookalikes, so the typosquat shape is corroborated. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.eclecticiq.com/luna-moth-callback-phishing-campaign-targets-us-legal-and-financial-firms • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1032/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/fbi-warns-silent-ransom-group-targets-law-firms-in-callback-phishing-attacks/
ATT&CKT1583.001 T1566.004

DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| where RemoteUrl has_any (HelpdeskDomains)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
let HelpdeskDomains = dynamic(["duanemorris-helpdesk.com","perkinscoie-helpdesk.com","millermartin-helpdesk.com"]);
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has_any (HelpdeskDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, ResultCodeName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] SRG in-person USB exfil: mass file copy to non-system drive after remote-help tool Actions on Objectives Medium
Catches the SRG fallback playbook — when the phone-based remote-desktop attempt fails, an SRG operative shows up in person and copies data via USB/external HDD. Looks for a burst of file writes to a non-C: drive shortly after a known remote-help binary executed on the same host. Rationale: Article explicitly states: 'SRG sends a threat actor to the victim's location to gain access to insert a storage device into the victim's computer' and 'steal data by connecting USB drives or external hard drives'. The remote-help tool list comes from EclecticIQ + prior FBI PIN documentation of Luna Moth's preferred RMM tooling (Zoho Assist, AnyDesk, Splashtop, Atera, Syncro). Cross-checked against: • https://blog.eclecticiq.com/luna-moth-callback-phishing-campaign-targets-us-legal-and-financial-firms • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/fbi-warns-silent-ransom-group-targets-law-firms-in-callback-phishing-attacks/
ATT&CKT1052.001 T1219 T1005

let RecentRemoteHelp = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where FileName in~ (RemoteHelpTools)

[LLM] SRG extortion leak-site contact: traffic to business-data-leaks.com Actions on Objectives High
Detects any outbound contact from a corporate endpoint to the SRG/Luna Moth public leak site business-data-leaks.com. A hit means either a victim navigating to verify a ransom threat, or an SRG-controlled host inside the network signalling/posting. Rationale: business-data-leaks.com is named in the article as the SRG-controlled leak site used to extort victims. Any outbound hit from a corp host is presumptively malicious or victim-impact-stage — extremely low base rate. Cross-checked with the May 2025 FBI PIN and EclecticIQ writeup which both reference Luna Moth's data-leak-site model. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.eclecticiq.com/luna-moth-callback-phishing-campaign-targets-us-legal-and-financial-firms • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/fbi-warns-silent-ransom-group-targets-law-firms-in-callback-phishing-attacks/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1657/
ATT&CKT1657 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web.Web
DeviceNetworkEvents

| where RemoteUrl has "business-data-leaks.com"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc

(DnsEvents
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(60d)

  | where RequestURL has "business-data-leaks.com" or DestinationHostName has "business-data-leaks.com"
  | project TimeGenerated, Host=SourceHostName, ClientIP=SourceIP, Indicator=coalesce(RequestURL, DestinationHostName), Source="Proxy")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator Delivery High
External Teams chat where displayName contains 'helpdesk' or 'IT support' — common 2024+ vishing pattern (Storm-1811, Black Basta, UNC6692). No CIM data model maps to Teams chats; uses raw O365 audit logs.
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1566
Data sourcesCloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"
| where RawEventData has "ExternalParticipants"
| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,
          ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
`o365_management_activity`
  Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation=MessageSent
  ExternalParticipants=*
| where match(SenderDisplayName, "(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)")
| stats count, earliest(_time) as firstTime, latest(_time) as lastTime
    by SenderUpn, SenderDisplayName, RecipientUpn, ChatId

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010

// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — GlassWorm Malware Takedown Disrupts Developer Supply Chain Attack Infrastructure
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] VS Code / Cursor child writes to Chrome extension directory (GlassWormRAT browser extension drop) · Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Hunts outbound connections to the four commercial-VPS C2 endpoints CrowdStrike/Shadowserver attributed to GlassWorm — one of the four resilient channels used by the JS RAT to receive instructions and exfil developer tokens. Article-specific because these IPs only appear in GlassWorm reporting. Rationale: Pre-extracted IOC list names exactly these four IPs; CrowdStrike's takedown writeup is the only public source citing them as GlassWorm direct C2, so any single hit is investigation-worthy regardless of process context.

[LLM] Solana mainnet RPC queried by VS Code / Cursor / Node.js (dead-drop resolver) Command & Control Medium
Hunts the GlassWorm Solana-blockchain dead-drop resolver: the malware queries Solana mainnet RPC endpoints to read C2 server addresses from memo fields of blockchain transactions. Article-specific because Solana RPC traffic from a code editor or its node.exe child is not legitimate developer behaviour outside Web3 teams. Rationale: Article explicitly names the Solana blockchain as the first of four C2 dead-drop channels — RPC queries to api.mainnet-beta.solana.com from a VS Code fork or its Node.js child is the exact behavioural footprint of the resolver fetching memo-field C2 addresses. Solana RPC hostnames are well documented in Solana's public docs.

[LLM] VS Code / Cursor child writes to Chrome extension directory (GlassWormRAT browser extension drop) Installation High
Hunts the secondary GlassWormRAT stage that installs a Google Chrome extension to harvest screenshots, keystrokes, and clipboard. The article specifies a code-editor-spawned process installs the Chrome extension, so writes into Chrome's Extensions folder by a non-Chrome process originating from a VS Code fork are the exact drop pattern. Rationale: Article states the RAT "install[s] a Google Chrome extension that, in turn, collects sensitive data, including screenshots, keystrokes, and clipboard content." Chrome unpacked-extension folders are only legitimately written by chrome.exe itself or by the Chrome Web Store updater — writes from a Node.js / code-editor child are an exact behavioural match for the GlassWormRAT browser-extension drop.

[LLM] Google Calendar API dead-drop polled by code-editor / Node process Command & Control Medium
Hunts the GlassWorm C2 channel that fetches the live C2 server address from Google Calendar event titles. Code editors and their Node.js helpers do not legitimately call the Calendar API — direct calls to calendar-v3 endpoints from these processes match the dead-drop fetch pattern. Rationale: Article explicitly states "Employing Google Calendar as a dead drop to fetch the C2 server address from event titles." Code editors / Node have no business calling the Calendar v3 API; the call is the resolver. Excluding fonts/storage googleapis paths removes the obvious legitimate Google traffic.

| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (DevEditors)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("calendar.google.com","googleapis.com/calendar","www.googleapis.com")
| where RemoteUrl !has "fonts.googleapis.com" and RemoteUrl !has "storage.googleapis.com" and RemoteUrl !has "chrome.googleapis.com"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort

[LLM] Developer credential & wallet file read by suspicious code-editor child Actions on Objectives High
Hunts the GlassWorm credential-harvesting stage that searches the host for GitHub / npm / OpenVSX tokens and crypto-wallet files. Reads of these specific secret paths by a Node / Python / PowerShell child of a code editor match Endor Labs' description of the searcher. Rationale: Endor Labs is quoted verbatim: "the malware searches the host for developer credentials (GitHub, NPM, OpenVSX tokens, crypto wallets)". Reading `\.config\gh\hosts.yml`, `.npmrc`, `.openvsx`, `.vsce`, and the named wallet directories from a code-editor-spawned child within a short window is precisely the searcher's footprint; requiring ≥2 distinct secret paths suppresses incidental single-file reads.
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1555 T1083
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
let SecretPaths = dynamic([@"\.npmrc", @"\.config\gh\hosts.yml", @"\AppData\Roaming\Exodus\", @"\AppData\Roaming\Electrum\wallets", @"\AppData\Roaming\Solana\", @"\AppData\Local\Coinbase Wallet\", @"\.openvsx\", @"\.vsce\", @"\AppData\Roaming\Code\User\globalStorage\", @"\AppData\Roaming\Cursor\User\globalStorage\", @"\.ssh\id_rsa", @"\.ssh\id_ed25519", @"wallet.dat", @"keystore"]);
let ChildProcs = dynamic(["node.exe","python.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","electron.exe"]);
let EditorParents = dynamic(["code.exe","cursor.exe","windsurf.exe","positron.exe","vscodium.exe"]);
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
   or (isnotempty(FolderPath))
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (ChildProcs)
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ (EditorParents)
| where FolderPath has_any (SecretPaths) or FileName in~ (".npmrc","wallet.dat","id_rsa","id_ed25519")
| summarize SecretsTouched=dcount(FolderPath), SamplePaths=make_set(FolderPath, 10), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| where SecretsTouched >= 2
| order by LastSeen desc
let SecretPaths = dynamic([@"\.npmrc", @"\.config\gh\hosts.yml", @"\AppData\Roaming\Exodus\", @"\AppData\Roaming\Electrum\wallets", @"\AppData\Roaming\Solana\", @"\AppData\Local\Coinbase Wallet\", @"\.openvsx\", @"\.vsce\", @"\AppData\Roaming\Code\User\globalStorage\", @"\.ssh\id_rsa", @"wallet.dat"]);
let ChildProcs = dynamic(["node.exe","python.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","electron.exe"]);
let EditorParents = dynamic(["code.exe","cursor.exe","windsurf.exe","positron.exe","vscodium.exe"]);
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any (ChildProcs)
| where TargetFilePath has_any (SecretPaths) or TargetFileName in~ (".npmrc","wallet.dat","id_rsa","id_ed25519")
| summarize SecretsTouched=dcount(TargetFilePath), SamplePaths=make_set(TargetFilePath, 10), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| where SecretsTouched >= 2
| order by LastSeen desc

#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo TargetFileName=/(\.npmrc|\\gh\\hosts\.yml|\\Exodus\\|\\Electrum\\wallets|\\Solana\\|Coinbase Wallet|\.openvsx|\.vsce|\.ssh\\id_(rsa|ed25519)|wallet\.dat)/i ContextImageFileName=/\\(node|python|powershell|pwsh|electron)\.exe$/i

[LLM] BitTorrent DHT bootstrap traffic from developer workstation Command & Control Medium
Hunts the third GlassWorm C2 resolver: BitTorrent DHT queries to retrieve configuration data. DHT bootstrap traffic (router.bittorrent.com / router.utorrent.com / dht.transmissionbt.com / UDP 6881-6889) from a developer workstation that has no torrent client installed is a strong indicator of the resolver running. Rationale: Article: "Querying the BitTorrent Distributed Hash Table (DHT) peer-to-peer network to retrieve configuration data". DHT bootstrap hostnames are well-known and public; a dev workstation with no installed torrent client speaking DHT is the resolver pattern. Pairing the DNS hit with UDP 6881-6999 from a code-editor child reduces FP from torrent users.
ATT&CKT1090.003 T1071 T1102
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
let DhtBootstrap = dynamic(["router.bittorrent.com","router.utorrent.com","dht.transmissionbt.com","dht.libtorrent.org","router.silotis.us","dht.aelitis.com"]);
let DevProcs = dynamic(["node.exe","code.exe","cursor.exe","windsurf.exe","positron.exe","vscodium.exe","electron.exe","python.exe"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where (RemoteUrl has_any (DhtBootstrap))
     or (Protocol == "Udp" and RemotePort between (6881 .. 6999) and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (DevProcs))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Protocol, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
let DhtBootstrap = dynamic(["router.bittorrent.com","router.utorrent.com","dht.transmissionbt.com","dht.libtorrent.org","router.silotis.us","dht.aelitis.com"]);
let DevProcs = dynamic(["node.exe","code.exe","cursor.exe","windsurf.exe","positron.exe","vscodium.exe","electron.exe","python.exe"]);
union
(ImDnsActivity
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
  | where DnsQuery in~ (DhtBootstrap)
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DnsQuery, Channel="DNS"),
(ImNetworkSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
  | where NetworkProtocol == "UDP" and DstPortNumber between (6881 .. 6999)
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Channel="DHT-UDP")
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: BitTorrent DHT Bootstrap From Developer Workstation (GlassWorm Resolver)
id: a3e1c5b8-2f47-4c0e-8d92-7f1a9e3b6c44
description: Detects DNS or UDP traffic to BitTorrent DHT bootstrap nodes from a workstation. GlassWorm uses DHT as one of four C2-resolver channels.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/glassworm-malware-takedown-disrupts.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/27
tags:
  - attack.t1071
  - attack.t1102
  - attack.command_and_control
logsource:
  category: dns
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    QueryName:
      - 'router.bittorrent.com'
      - 'router.utorrent.com'
      - 'dht.transmissionbt.com'
      - 'dht.libtorrent.org'
      - 'router.silotis.us'
      - 'dht.aelitis.com'
  condition: selection
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon ((@EventID:22 @QueryName:(router.bittorrent.com OR router.utorrent.com OR dht.transmissionbt.com OR dht.libtorrent.org OR router.silotis.us OR dht.aelitis.com)) OR (@EventID:3 @Protocol:udp @DestinationPort:[6881 TO 6999] @Image:(*\\node.exe OR *\\Node.exe OR *\\code.exe OR *\\Code.exe OR *\\cursor.exe OR *\\windsurf.exe OR *\\electron.exe OR *\\python.exe)))
(#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/^(router\.bittorrent\.com|router\.utorrent\.com|dht\.transmissionbt\.com|dht\.libtorrent\.org|router\.silotis\.us|dht\.aelitis\.com)$/i)
OR (#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 Protocol=17 RemotePort>=6881 RemotePort<=6999 ContextImageFileName=/\\(node|code|cursor|windsurf|positron|vscodium|electron|python)\.exe$/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, DomainName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where DNS.query IN ("router.bittorrent.com","router.utorrent.com","dht.transmissionbt.com","dht.libtorrent.org","router.silotis.us","dht.aelitis.com") by DNS.src, DNS.query | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)` | append [ | tstats summariesonly=true count from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port>=6881 All_Traffic.dest_port<=6999 All_Traffic.transport="udp" All_Traffic.app IN ("node.exe","code.exe","cursor.exe","windsurf.exe","python.exe","electron.exe") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.app All_Traffic.dest_ip All_Traffic.dest_port | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` ]
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where DNS.query IN ("router.bittorrent.com","router.utorrent.com","dht.transmissionbt.com","dht.libtorrent.org","router.silotis.us","dht.aelitis.com") by DNS.src, DNS.query | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)` | append [ | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port>=6881 All_Traffic.dest_port<=6999 All_Traffic.transport="udp" All_Traffic.app IN ("node.exe","code.exe","cursor.exe","windsurf.exe","python.exe","electron.exe") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.app All_Traffic.dest_ip All_Traffic.dest_port | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` ]
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

3 SOC Steps that Shut Down Incident Risks Early

The Hacker News
2026-05-27 10 use cases 5 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Most organizations still picture cyber defense as a fortress problem: build stronger walls, add more guards, buy another detection engine. But modern incidents rarely crash through the front gate. They drift in disguised as routine activity, hide inside legitimate processes, and quietly accumulate risk long before anyone labels them an "incident." That changes the role of the SOC entirely. Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

         by Processes.dest, Processes.user

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Gitea Vulnerability Exposes Private Container Images without Authentication

The Hacker News
2026-05-27 8 use cases 4 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed a security flaw in Gitea, an open-source, self-hosted platform for version control, that allows unauthenticated remote attackers to pull private container images from Gitea deployments without requiring an account, password, or other credentials. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-27771 (CVSS score: N/A), affects all versions of Gitea prior to 1.26.2

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Anonymous Gitea OCI registry pull (/v2/...manifests|blobs) — CVE-2026-27771 exploitation · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children

[LLM] Vulnerable Gitea / Forgejo instance exposed to CVE-2026-27771 Reconnaissance High
Identifies self-hosted Gitea (and forks like Forgejo) running a version below 1.26.2, which allows unauthenticated pulls of private container images via the OCI v2 registry endpoints. Pure asset-hunting UC to surface unpatched instances before the exploit pattern fires. Rationale: Pins on the explicit CVE-2026-27771 identifier and the article's named fix version (1.26.2) — also captures the Noscope-confirmed Forgejo fork. Cross-checked against Noscope's advisory (https://www.noscope.com/blog/gitea-instances-exposing-private-container) and Gitea's security page. Falcon/Datadog/CloudWatch queries left empty — these vendor inventory feeds don't ship Gitea version data by default; the vuln-mgmt tables on MDE/Sentinel and Splunk's Vulnerabilities datamodel are where this lives. Cross-checked against: • https://www.noscope.com/blog/gitea-instances-exposing-private-container • https://about.gitea.com/security • https://docs.gitea.com/usage/packages/container
